title: How fast is Helsinki spinning?
hook: The spinning Earth carries you east all day. Is everyone going the same speed?

knows: that the Earth spins about once a day
latitude in degrees north of the equator
doesNotKnow: that your speed from the spin depends on your latitude
that circles of latitude shrink toward the poles

misconception: Everyone on Earth is carried around at the same speed, about 1,670 km/h.
objective: The learner can explain that everyone makes one turn in the same time, but the circle of latitude shrinks with cos(latitude), so Helsinki (60°N) moves about half as fast as the equator (about 830 vs 1,670 km/h).
keyState: The equator and Helsinki have both been visited, with their circles, arrows and speeds shown.

claims.text: Earth's spin carries someone on the equator at about 1,670 km/h.
claims.source: v = 2πR / T with R = 6,371.0088 km (mean radius) and T = 86,164.09 s (sidereal day): 1,672.5 km/h. Demo.tsx speed(0). On the WGS84 ellipsoid the equatorial radius 6,378.137 km gives 1,674.4 km/h (cm-geography brief), so 'about 1,670' holds either way. Speed is relative to Earth's axis (not to the Sun or the galaxy). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Node: 1,672.5 km/h on the sphere with a sidereal day; shown as 1,670.

claims.text: In Helsinki (60°N) the spin carries you at about 830 km/h, about half the equator's speed.
claims.source: speed(60.17) = 1,672.5 × cos 60.17° = 831.9 km/h (builder node run; Demo.tsx). Ratio 0.497. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Node: 831.9 km/h at 60.17 N; shown as 830.

claims.text: Everyone goes round once in the same time, 23 h 56 min (one sidereal day).
claims.source: Sidereal day 86,164.09 s = 23 h 56 min 4 s (IERS conventions; from memory). The solar day (24 h) is the turn relative to the Sun; speed relative to the axis uses the sidereal day. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Sidereal day 23 h 56 min 4 s.

claims.text: The circle of latitude at Helsinki is about 19,910 km round, against 40,030 km at the equator.
claims.source: 2πR cos φ on the sphere R = 6,371.0088 km: 19,912 km at 60.17°N, 40,030 km at 0° (Demo.tsx circleKm). The real equator is 40,075 km on WGS84 (from memory). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Node: 19,912 and 40,030 km; shown as 19,910 and 40,030.

claims.text: A circle of latitude shrinks with the cosine of the latitude; cos 60° is one half.
claims.source: The radius of the parallel at latitude φ on a sphere is R cos φ (geometry). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Re-derived; no issue.

claims.text: At the North Pole you just turn on the spot.
claims.source: cos 90° = 0: the circle has zero radius. Quoted in the reveal only if the learner visited the pole. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Re-derived; no issue.

claims.text: Helsinki is at about 60°N; London at about 51.5°N.
claims.source: Gazetteer coordinates (from memory): Helsinki 60.17°N, London 51.51°N. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Helsinki 60.17 N, London 51.51 N.

recall.question: Two people stand on the spinning Earth, one on the equator and one at 60°N. Who is carried faster, and by how much?
options: Same speed: the Earth turns as one
The equator person, about twice as fast
The 60°N person, being nearer the axis
recall.why: Both make one turn in the same time, but the circle at 60°N is half as long (cos 60° = 1/2), so it moves about half as fast.
